conceptFrozenBeforeSelection.concept: Digital security, governance and cybercrime inquiry
conceptFrozenBeforeSelection.targetBasis: Cybersecurity is a socio-technical problem: technical operation and protection of networked systems, offending/victimisation and legal enforcement, organisational/public governance and evidence-based response. Build a programme-level closest challenge integrating these objects rather than a generic computer-science or social-science bundle.

candidateDirections.name: Digital security, governance and cybercrime inquiry
candidateDirections.role: Strongest closest response; defining target remains cyber threats and social/legal response.

candidateDirections.name: Cyber risk, public policy and organisational resilience
candidateDirections.role: Coherent core reorganisation, tested only after closest gate; generic management alone is insufficient.

candidateDirections.name: Technical systems and digital evidence
candidateDirections.role: Coherent technical/evidence reorganisation; ordinary software/machine-learning content does not establish attack/defence or forensic practice by itself.

conceptFrozenBeforeSelection.ownership: All16generator-eligible interests owned by defining multidisciplinary core; candidate directions reorganise them and do not invent extra interests or residual category.
conceptFrozenBeforeSelection.stopping: No accepted comparison or extra alternative before unresolved external30EC and full programme comparability are established. No three-slot target, no arbitrary four-course swaps, no final no-match from missing source/planning.

screening: Screened all151active current workbook rows, then read40plausible technical, legal, governance, empirical, psychological, communication and organisational leads in substance. Life science/environment/arts rows without target objects were not selected. Course evidence and provenance stay internal.

courseLedger.name: Personal & Professional Development

availableEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
availableEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
availableEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courseLedger.contribution: Academic communication, information literacy, civic reflection and research habits.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Mandatory PPD in year1; supports scholarly practice, not substantive cyber coverage.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Programming

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
availableEvidence.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
availableEvidence.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

courseLedger.contribution: Python functions, programming constructs and tested computational problem solving.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Direct technical foundation; not a full attack/defence course.

courseLedger.name: Mathematical Methods

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
availableEvidence.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
availableEvidence.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Calculus foundations and quantitative problem solving.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Prerequisite route for probability; not by itself cryptography or cyber relevance.

courseLedger.name: Networks & Operating Systems

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces computer networks and operating systems. Covers how the internet works and the role of an OS in resource management and application support.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies computer networks and operating systems as the infrastructure for communication and resource management. Internet protocols are examined through the application, transport, network and link layers. Operating-system study covers processes, threads, scheduling, concurrency, memory and persistent storage. Wireshark laboratories and investigative projects connect these concepts to observed packet behaviour, network properties and experimental examination of operating-system performance.
availableEvidence.discipline: Computer science; Computer networking; Operating systems
availableEvidence.topics: Internet architecture; HTTP and DNS; UDP and TCP; IPv4 and IPv6; Network address translation; Network data and control planes; Ethernet and ARP; Processes and threads; CPU scheduling; Virtualization; Synchronization and deadlocks; Memory management; Storage and file systems
availableEvidence.methods: Network packet capture and analysis with Wireshark; Experimental investigation of network and operating-system behaviour; Hypothesis-based performance testing; Sensitivity analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Operating systems, memory/storage/concurrency, Internet protocol layers and Wireshark packet analysis.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Strong concrete system/network object; packet analysis is not certified digital-forensic or penetration-test training.

courseLedger.name: Database Management Systems

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.

courseLedger.contribution: Description supports relational databases, SQL, authorisation, normalisation and query processing.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Full consideration despite description-only status; authorisation is relevant, not an inferred security laboratory.

courseLedger.name: Software Development

availableEvidence.description2: Covers software design, creation, testing and maintenance. Uses C++ and Haskell and covers planning, requirements gathering, testing, deployment and maintenance through discussions and code reviews.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops software-construction skills through C++ and functional programming in Haskell, alongside software design and quality assurance. C++ work addresses classes, inheritance, polymorphism and memory management; Haskell introduces functions, recursion, types and input/output. Laboratories apply version control, code review, debugging, testing, documentation and design patterns. Projects require students to build and explain programs in both languages.
availableEvidence.topics: C++ classes and operator overloading; Inheritance and polymorphism; Dynamic memory and smart pointers; Copy construction; Functional programming and immutability; Haskell functions, recursion and types; Higher-order functions; Software development lifecycle; Version control; Debugging and testing; Documentation; Design patterns
availableEvidence.methods: C++ programming; Haskell functional programming; Git and GitLab version control; Code review; Systematic debugging; Unit and integration testing; White-box and black-box testing; Static testing; Design-pattern implementation; Software documentation

courseLedger.contribution: C++/Haskell, version control, testing, code review and software quality.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Useful implementation discipline; secure coding and cyber-defence testing not established.

courseLedger.name: Algorithms & Data Structures

availableEvidence.description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
availableEvidence.discipline: Computer science; Algorithm design and analysis; Computational complexity
availableEvidence.topics: Abstract data structures; Asymptotic complexity; Random-number generation and sampling; Sorting and stability; String matching and finite automata; Sequential and binary search; Graph traversal; Shortest paths and spanning trees; Topological sorting; Computability and Turing machines; Polynomial-time verification; Reductions and complexity hierarchy
availableEvidence.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions

courseLedger.contribution: Graph/string algorithms, complexity and experimental benchmarking.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Supports computational analysis of networked problems; not a cyberattack curriculum by algorithm title.

courseLedger.name: Advanced Algorithms

availableEvidence.description2: Studies modern algebraic algorithms and optimization methods. Emphasises algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling of computational problems.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies algebraic algorithms and advanced optimization methods through mathematical reasoning, implementation and experimental analysis. Fast and exact arithmetic, number-theoretic algorithms, matrix multiplication and Fourier transformation lead into hashing, greedy methods, dynamic programming and network flows. Laboratories develop algorithmic understanding, while projects investigate exact computing and optimization, including hypotheses, measured performance and sensitivity analysis.
availableEvidence.discipline: Computer science; Algorithm design and analysis; Computational mathematics
availableEvidence.topics: Asymptotic time complexity; Fast integer arithmetic; Greatest common divisors and modular arithmetic; Chinese remainder theorem; Arbitrary-precision integers; Primality and factorization; Fast matrix multiplication; Polynomials and Fourier transformation; Hashing and Bloom filters; Greedy algorithms and coding; Dynamic programming; Flow networks; Network science
availableEvidence.methods: Asymptotic and empirical complexity analysis; Euclidean algorithm; Primality testing and factorization; Fast arithmetic and matrix algorithms; Fast Fourier transformation; Hashing; Greedy optimization; Dynamic programming; Maximum-flow algorithms; Algorithmic experimental design; Sensitivity analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Number theory, hashing, flow algorithms and sensitivity reasoning.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Potential analytic tools; no claim of a full cryptography/security course.

courseLedger.name: AI Ethics

availableEvidence.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
availableEvidence.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
availableEvidence.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing

courseLedger.contribution: Privacy, surveillance, fairness, accountability and forensic-AI psychology, using ethics inquiry and a podcast.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Concrete digital governance and social consequences; not criminal-investigation practice.

courseLedger.name: Decision-making in AI

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops the mathematical foundations of intelligent-agent decisions under uncertainty. Probability and Bayesian networks support belief updating and inference, while temporal models address changing environments. Decision theory, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems connect uncertainty to policies and expected utility. Multi-agent decisions introduce strategic and collective interaction, and probabilistic programming provides a framework for expressing models. Students work through equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.
availableEvidence.discipline: Artificial intelligence; Probability; Decision theory; Game theory
availableEvidence.topics: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule; Bayesian networks; Temporal probabilistic models; Hidden Markov models and dynamic Bayesian networks; Expected utility; Markov and partially observable decision processes; Exploration-exploitation trade-offs and bandits; Competitive and cooperative multi-agent interaction; Negotiation, auctions and voting; Probabilistic programming
availableEvidence.methods: Probabilistic inference; Bayesian-network modelling; Temporal probabilistic modelling; Expected-utility analysis; Sequential decision modelling; Game-theoretic analysis; Probabilistic programming

courseLedger.contribution: Bayesian/probabilistic and temporal reasoning, MDPs and game-theoretic uncertainty.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Decision tools for risk questions; no promised cyber incident-response protocol.

courseLedger.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics

availableEvidence.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
availableEvidence.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
availableEvidence.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling

courseLedger.contribution: Proof, Boolean logic, circuits and process/game reasoning.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Logical and technical foundation, not substantive crime/defence instruction.

courseLedger.name: Optimization Methods in AI

availableEvidence.description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies search and optimization for rational agents in known, complex and adversarial environments. Students move from uninformed and heuristic search to local and global optimization, first- and second-order methods and population approaches. Adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimization extend the toolkit. Laboratories and projects require algorithm tracing, implementation and evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
availableEvidence.discipline: Artificial intelligence; Mathematical optimization; Computer science
availableEvidence.topics: Intelligent and rational agents; Uninformed and informed search; Heuristic functions; Search in complex environments; Local and global optimization; First- and second-order optimization; Population methods; Adversarial games; Constraint satisfaction; Linear programming; Discrete optimization
availableEvidence.methods: Uninformed and heuristic search; Local and global search; First- and second-order optimization; Population-based optimization; Adversarial search; Monte Carlo tree search; Constraint-satisfaction algorithms; Linear programming; Discrete optimization; Algorithm implementation and experimental evaluation

courseLedger.contribution: Adversarial search, constraints, optimisation and linear programming.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Adversarial computational methods do not alone establish cyberattack objects; considered but displaced by actual statistical-design depth.

courseLedger.name: Reinforcement Learning

availableEvidence.description2: Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural networks that learn through trial and error.

courseLedger.contribution: Description supports reinforcement-learning agents, neural methods and trial/error learning.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Considered fully; no evidence of a cyber-defence application or forensic practice.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Data Science

availableEvidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
availableEvidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
availableEvidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courseLedger.contribution: R data cleaning/analysis, text, spatial data and web scraping.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Actual empirical tools; no claim of compulsory cyber datasets.

courseLedger.name: Machine Learning

availableEvidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
availableEvidence.discipline: Machine learning; Statistical learning; Data science
availableEvidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
availableEvidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

courseLedger.contribution: Predictive modelling, validation and machine-learning interpretation.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Analytic complement for threat/human data questions; cyber detection remains a proposed application, not taught content.

courseLedger.name: Probability & Statistics

availableEvidence.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
availableEvidence.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
availableEvidence.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
availableEvidence.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

courseLedger.contribution: Probability, inference and Monte Carlo modelling.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Substantive statistical option requiring DISGATE102; selected applied statistics instead, not excluded for planning alone.

courseLedger.name: Law, Society & Justice

availableEvidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
availableEvidence.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
availableEvidence.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

courseLedger.contribution: Legal/social control, legal institutions and IRAC/moot reasoning.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Coherent foundation for criminal/international/EU progression.

courseLedger.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy

availableEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
availableEvidence.discipline: Human rights law; Legal philosophy; Ethics
availableEvidence.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
availableEvidence.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Rights including expression, dignity and punishment.
courseLedger.limitAndSelection: Rights context relevant to privacy/security debate; not a complete digital-data code.

courseLedger.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice

availableEvidence.description2: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines the principles of criminal liability and the legal and moral bases of criminal justice. Students study criminal acts, causation and mental elements, legality, punishment, criminalization, justifications, excuses, inchoate offences and participation.
